The Senegal coucal (Centropus senegalensis) exhibits a well-defined incubation period that has been documented under controlled captive conditions. Eggs maintained at a stable temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] typically hatch after approximately 18.5 days [ab = approximately 18.5 days], a developmental duration that aligns closely with what has been reported among congeners of similar body size. The mass of the freshly laid egg, which represents the wet weight at birth in this species, averages 12.3 grams [Wwb = 12.3 grams]. This modest initial mass belies the rapid post-hatching growth trajectory characteristic of altricial nestlings that are heavily dependent on biparental care. The incubation temperature of 36.2 °C falls within the range typical for many tropical cuckoo species, reflecting a balance between embryonic development rates and the thermal demands of the external environment. Field records suggest that this incubation regime is consistent across the species' range in sub-Saharan Africa.

Under the elevated thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of this species, approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones becomes evident. Fledging, defined as the age at which the juvenile achieves sustained flight and leaves the nest, occurs at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This represents a relatively rapid attainment of flight capability compared to other cuckoo species, potentially linked to high predation pressure in its savanna and woodland habitats. Following fledging, the young coucal enters a period of continued growth and feather maturation, during which it remains dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks. The relatively short nestling phase of this species is indicative of its life-history strategy, favoring rapid development to reduce the period of vulnerability within the nest.

Sexual maturity in the Senegal coucal is attained at 57 days after hatching [tp = 57 days after hatching] when the birds are maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a developmental pace that is notably accelerated when compared to many temperate-zone cuckoos. This early onset of gonadal activation allows young birds to enter the breeding population within their first year, a trait that may be advantageous in the unpredictable tropical environments the species inhabits. The ultimate body mass achieved by adult females reaches 171 grams [Wwi = 171 grams], whereas males, which are slightly smaller, attain a maximum weight of 169 grams [Wwi = 169 grams]. This modest sexual dimorphism in size is common among coucals and is thought to be related to the species' social system, where males contribute substantially to offspring care.

The first successful breeding event in the Senegal coucal typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This pattern of deferred first reproduction, occurring after the individual has reached full adult body mass, allows for the accumulation of sufficient somatic reserves to support the high energetic demands of nesting. The reproductive output per event is modest, with females laying 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch]. Field studies indicate that this species usually produces a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a relatively low annual investment that may reflect constraints on foraging efficiency or the costs of extended parental care typical of coucals.

Maximum longevity in the Senegal coucal has been estimated at approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years], extrapolated from survivorship data for related Cuculus canoris and reported at a standard metabolic temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This lifespan is consistent with the slow life-history pace of many tropical non-passerine birds, which typically exhibit lower annual mortality rates than their temperate counterparts. The species' single annual clutch of 3 eggs, modest adult mass of 171 grams in females, and maximum lifetime of 9 years together position it along a conservative life-history continuum. Population viability analyses would benefit from integrating these demographic parameters to assess how environmental variability affects recruitment and persistence across its fragmented West African range.
